question: A travel-booking assistant developer wants to cut latency by sending only the user's latest message plus a one-sentence rolling summary on each API call, rather than the full prior turns. Ten turns into a session, the customer says "book the same seat type I mentioned earlier," but the assistant no longer has access to that detail because it was dropped from the rolling summary. What is the underlying issue?
options: A) The rolling summary approach fails only because it was one sentence long; a two- or three-sentence summary would retain the seat type
B) The model's built-in conversational memory should have retained the seat preference across calls without it being resent
C) The customer should have repeated the seat preference on every subsequent turn to guarantee it stays available
D) The API treats each request as stateless, so any turn left out of the message history sent with it is unavailable to the model
correct_answers: D) The API treats each request as stateless, so any turn left out of the message history sent with it is unavailable to the model
explanations: Lengthening the rolling summary might help this one case but does not address the root cause: any compression scheme can drop an arbitrary detail depending on wording and length limits.
There is no persistent memory between separate API calls; assuming otherwise is the mistake that caused the failure.
Requiring the customer to repeat themselves works around the symptom but blames the user for a context-management problem the application should have solved.
Correct — the API does not retain memory between separate requests; every fact the model needs, including details from turn one, must be present in the message history sent with the current request.
